p: Yes—think of Michelangelo as the center of several overlapping networks. Below, each arrow names the connection; importantly, some people also connect directly to one another.
Michelangelo — brother of → Buonarroto — father of → Lionardo, Michelangelo’s nephew and principal heir.
This was also a financial network: Michelangelo supported relatives, helped with property and marriage arrangements, and worried about preserving the family’s standing.
h2: 2. The Medici: family ties became patronage ties
p: Lorenzo de’ Medici — early protector of → Michelangelo.
Lorenzo — father of → Leo X, and uncle of → Clement VII. The two future popes were first cousins; both later commissioned Michelangelo.

Bertoldo di Giovanni also belonged to Lorenzo’s artistic circle. Through the Medici sculpture garden, the young Michelangelo encountered Bertoldo and ancient sculpture. Bertoldo’s precise role as a formal teacher is less certain than this shared setting.

The tension: Medici protection advanced Michelangelo’s career, but he later helped defend republican Florence against the family’s restoration in 1529–1530. Patronage did not mean unconditional political loyalty.

td.p: Commissioned the Pietà now in Saint Peter’s.
Commissioned his own monumental tomb and the Sistine Chapel ceiling: an enormously productive but frequently strained relationship.
Commissioned the unrealized façade of San Lorenzo and helped initiate the Medici funerary project.
Advanced the Medici Chapel and Laurentian Library projects, then initiated the Last Judgment commission.
Supported completion of the Last Judgment, commissioned the Pauline Chapel frescoes, and appointed Michelangelo architect of Saint Peter’s.

p: Earlier in Rome, Cardinal Riario helped occasion Michelangelo’s arrival through the sleeping-Cupid affair, while Jacopo Galli became a supporter and intermediary. They were different kinds of connections—not all patrons simply placed a famous commission.

li.p: Ghirlandaio — master of the workshop where he apprenticed → Michelangelo. Granacci was a fellow artist and lasting friend from his youth.
Leonardo da Vinci ↔ Michelangelo: rival contemporaries, particularly through their competing Florentine battle-mural projects—not teacher and pupil.
Raphael ↔ Michelangelo: rivals sharing papal patrons. Raphael absorbed Michelangelo’s artistic example, but was not his apprentice.
Michelangelo — supplied designs and artistic support to → Sebastiano del Piombo. Their collaboration also positioned Sebastiano as a competitor to Raphael.
Michelangelo — provided designs used in paintings by → Marcello Venusti and Pontormo.

Montorsoli and Raffaello da Montelupo — assisted Michelangelo on sculptural projects. Daniele da Volterra was a close younger artistic associate; after Michelangelo’s death, he added coverings to figures in the Last Judgment.

p: Vittoria Colonna ↔ Michelangelo: close friendship, poetry and religious exchange.
Tommaso de’ Cavalieri ↔ Michelangelo: deep personal attachment, expressed through poems and gift drawings. The surviving evidence does not settle the exact private nature of their relationship.
Urbino → Michelangelo: trusted servant, assistant and household companion.
Condivi and Vasari → Michelangelo: personal acquaintances and biographers. Their writings connect the historical man to the heroic image inherited by later generations.

The geographical pattern: Florence connects family, training, the Medici and republican politics; Rome connects popes, artistic rivalry and much of his later personal circle; Carrara connects these ambitions to the practical business of obtaining marble.
